name: Nikhil Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Northgate Motor Factors, a distributor that supplies car parts to independent garages: brake pads, filters, bulbs, batteries. I'm a junior buyer, so I handle filters and wipers, the high-volume cheap stuff. My morning is checking yesterday's sales against stock, then ordering from three or four suppliers, and the afternoon is sorting problems when a delivery's short. I like the garages and their banter, and I don't like how often our system says we have stock we don't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. The other buyers started using an AI assistant to write supplier emails and I followed once I saw it worked. I'm still learning the job, so my manager, Rob, checks my orders before they go. I'm on lower pay than the others, I live with my girlfriend Sofia, who works early shifts at a bakery, and we've got maybe three weeks of money saved. There's not many jobs like mine round here, so I want to hang on to this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it means hard work still counts. I'd tell the lads at five-a-side on Thursday that the garages still want a real person on the phone. I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I'd still be on low pay with not much saved. Sofia and I want to buy a house one day, and right now that's a joke. AI not changing anything doesn't fix house prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the job and get better, so Rob stops checking every order. I'd keep using the AI for emails now and then. And I'd ask about overtime in the warehouse on Saturdays to put money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit stuck, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does stuck feel like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like watching my mates who went into trades buy vans and houses while I'm sorting wiper blades. My cousin Jas is a mechanic and earns more than me at twenty-four. It makes me wonder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever switch into a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I could afford the apprentice wage. That's the problem. You can't live on it with rent.

say: I'd say AI fizzling means **hard work** still counts.
I'd tell the lads at **five-a-side** that garages still want a real person on the phone.
think: I'd still be on **low pay** with little saved.
A **house** with Sofia feels like a joke at current prices.
do: Get better so **Rob stops** checking every order.
Keep using the **AI assistant** for emails now and then.
Ask for **Saturday overtime** in the warehouse.
S0.quote: My cousin Jas is a mechanic and earns more than me at twenty-four. It makes me wonder.
fieldNote: Nikhil's frustration is **low pay** and house prices, not AI.
He compares himself with **friends in trades** who earn more.
He'd use AI tools **once proven** by colleagues.

steps.text: Cut order mistakes so Rob stops checking every order
Use the AI assistant for supplier emails
Take Saturday overtime in the Northgate warehouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how markets work, new tech comes in and people adjust. I'd say firms should train people up, apprenticeships, not just cut them. I'd say that at work and to my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Northgate cuts a buyer and I'm the obvious one. Filters and wipers are just numbers for AI. My manager Rob has the garage contacts, so Rob stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI properly, every day, and ask Rob to show me how he deals with the big garage accounts, because that's the part that lasts. I'd also talk to my cousin Jas about an apprenticeship at his garage, especially on electric cars. Sofia and I would cut back to save for the apprentice wage gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Not panicking, but I wouldn't sleep great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electric cars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the garages we supply are all saying they can't find people who can work on them. It's hands-on and there's demand. Robots doing that are years off, I reckon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, maybe, since I could walk to Northgate. The football subs. Sofia would pick up a Saturday shift at the bakery.

say: I'd say this is how **markets work**: new tech arrives and people adjust.
I'd say firms should **train people up** with apprenticeships, not just cut them.
think: Northgate cuts a buyer and I'm **the obvious one**.
Filters and wipers are **just numbers** for AI; Rob's contacts keep him safe.
do: Use the **AI every day** and learn how Rob handles big garage accounts.
Ask Jas about an **electric car** apprenticeship at his garage.
Cut back on the **car** and football subs.
S1.quote: Filters and wipers are just numbers for AI. My manager Rob has the garage contacts, so Rob stays.
fieldNote: Nikhil frames change as **markets working**, yet expects to be the cut.
He picks **electric vehicles** because garages are short of people.
He'd lean on **family** for the apprenticeship route.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant daily and learn Rob's account work
Ask Jas about an electric car apprenticeship at his garage
Sell the car and drop the football subs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and people need to pull together, families, communities. I'm not big on handouts, but I'd want the government to help firms keep people on. I'd keep my head down at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk job at the parts distributor is gone by 2028, no question. Even my manager's probably gone. But garage work is hands-on, so if I'm in an electric car apprenticeship, I'd have until about 2031 before robots, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship with Jas's garage as soon as they'd take me, even on apprentice pay. Sofia and I would move in with my parents to make it work. I'd sell the car and anything else we don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with something to do. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents feel about you both moving in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say that's what family's for. My mum would make too much food. Sofia's fine with them, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots can do garage work too, around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-two and fully qualified. Maybe I'd be fixing the robots. I don't know, honestly.

say: I'd say people should **pull together** as families and communities.
I'd want the government to help firms **keep people** on, not give handouts.
think: My desk job is **gone by 2028**, and probably Rob's too.
An **apprenticeship** gives me until about 2031 before robots.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** at Jas's garage on apprentice pay.
Move in with **my parents** with Sofia.
**Sell the car** and anything else we don't need.
S2.quote: My desk job at the parts distributor is gone by 2028, no question. Even my manager's probably gone.
fieldNote: Nikhil is **clear-eyed** that buying vanishes in two years.
He uses the **robot gap** to start an apprenticeship at once.
Family is his **safety net**, in line with his views.

steps.text: Start an electric car apprenticeship at Jas's garage
Move in with his parents along with Sofia
Lean on his parents for housing during training
Sell the car and spare belongings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people get on with it. Apprenticeships, learning, no moaning. I'd say that at work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the buying job goes around 2031, so I've got a few years. I'd start the apprenticeship in a year or two and be qualified by 2031. Garage work lasts till about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd stay at Northgate, save hard, and do a short evening course on electric car basics. I'd ask Jas's garage to take me on next year. Sofia and I would put off moving in together properly until I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but okay. It's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off moving in. Aren't you living together already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We are, in a rented room in a shared house. I meant getting our own flat. That would wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Northgate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob, honestly. My manager at the parts distributor is fifty-two and would be competing with AI that does his job. He's been good to me.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if people get on with it.
I'd say apprenticeships and learning beat **moaning**.
think: The buying job goes around **2031**, so I have a few years.
I'd be **qualified** by 2031, and garage work lasts till about 2034.
do: Stay at Northgate, **save hard**, and take an evening EV course.
Ask Jas's garage to take me on **next year**.
Put off getting **our own flat** until qualified.
S3.quote: My manager at the parts distributor is fifty-two and would be competing with AI that does his job. He's been good to me.
fieldNote: Five years gives Nikhil a **staged move** into garage work.
He worries for his **manager Rob**, who is older and exposed.
Housing plans go on **hold** while he trains.

steps.text: Save hard while working at Northgate
Take an evening course on electric car basics
Delay getting their own flat until qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so no need to panic. Learn a trade or get really good at what you do. That's what I'd tell my younger brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could get good at buying, maybe get promoted, and still move into garage work later. Or stay if buying changes into something else. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd focus on the job and use AI more, like the others. I'd save for a flat with Sofia. I'd think about the apprenticeship in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Still thinking about money, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you it's time to switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Northgate stops hiring buyers and starts hiring people to run the software. That's the sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sixteen-year-old brother to do an apprenticeship straight from school, not a desk job like mine.

I'd tell my brother to learn a **trade** or get really good at his work.

do: Focus on the job and use **AI more**, like the others.
Consider the **apprenticeship** in a few years.
S4.quote: I'd tell my sixteen-year-old brother to do an apprenticeship straight from school, not a desk job like mine.
fieldNote: With ten years Nikhil's worry fades to **background unease**.
His clearest advice goes to his **younger brother**: trades over desks.
He has a **clear signal** to switch: Northgate hiring software staff.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant daily at Northgate

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be starting an apprenticeship with no money and a girlfriend depending on me. What would help is apprentice wages adults can live on, and firms paying to train their own people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what we'd tell younger people. I'd tell kids not to do what I did, sitting at a screen. Learn something with your hands.

headlineQuote: I'd tell kids not to do what I did, sitting at a screen. Learn something with your hands.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old** junior buyer of filters and wipers at a car parts distributor.
He uses AI **now and then**, once colleagues proved it worked.
He and girlfriend Sofia live in a **rented room** with about three weeks of savings.
In most pictures he plans an **electric car** apprenticeship at his cousin's garage.
He believes in **markets and family**, and would lean on his parents rather than government.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be starting an apprenticeship with no money.
whatWouldHelp: Apprentice wages **adults can live on**, and firms paying to train their own staff.
